title: 437 MHz 9-element long-Yagi
summary: Nine-element DL6WU long-Yagi for the 70 cm band, designed to feed 50 Ω directly with only a 1:1 balun, and documented as a full construction manual.
details: Designed a 9-element Rothammel/DL6WU long-Yagi for 437 MHz: 1283 mm round-boom array of one reflector, a straight half-wave dipole and seven directors, calculated for 11.24 dBd (13.39 dBi) over 428–446 MHz
Sized the driven element from theory rather than by trial: a 343 mm half-wave scaled by a 0.959 thickness-correction factor to two 164.6 mm halves across a 3.4 mm feed gap
Eliminated the matching network by choosing a straight dipole over a folded one, putting the feedpoint near 50 Ω so only a 1:1 balun is needed instead of an impedance step-up

Carried the boom diameter through the calculation as a design variable (d/λ = 0.007, D/λ = 0.015), so element lengths and the 51→216 mm progressive director spacing stay valid for the 10 mm round boom actually used

title: Five-phase IPMSM field-oriented control
summary: Dual-plane field-oriented control of a five-phase IPMSM, taken from an open-loop machine model to a closed-loop drive with five PID loops and five-phase SVPWM, then to ePWM on TI C2000 hardware.
details: Built a five-phase IPMSM model in Simulink with dual-plane Clarke/Park transforms, resolving the machine into a fundamental (d1-q1) and a third-harmonic (d3-q3) plane rather than the single plane a three-phase drive needs
Implemented torque production across both planes, including the reluctance term (Ld−Lq)·id·iq and the third-harmonic contribution, so injected third-harmonic current adds torque instead of only loss
Closed five control loops — one speed loop and four current loops — and tuned them with Simulink's Closed-Loop PID Autotuner against the plant model
Generated gate signals with five-phase space-vector PWM, driving a 10-switch two-level inverter at a 2 µs discrete step
Derived loss-aware MTPA with Lagrange multipliers and solved it numerically with Newton-Raphson, and implemented direct torque control with 20-sector hysteresis switching as a comparison scheme
Ported the modulator to a TI C2000 DSP in Code Composer Studio, generating ePWM and testing the gate driver circuit

sections.heading: The problem
sections.body:
A three-phase drive has one current plane and two degrees of freedom. A five-phase machine has two planes and four, and most of the extra freedom is usually thrown away — the third-harmonic plane is treated as a loss path to be suppressed rather than a place to make torque.

Five-phase machines are used where a lost phase must not stop the machine, so the control has to be built around that structure from the start rather than bolted on afterwards. The question I wanted to answer was what it actually takes to control both planes at once, and whether the second plane earns its complexity.

sections.heading: Approach
sections.body:
I built the drive in two stages rather than one.

The first model excites the machine open-loop with sinusoidal voltages and verifies the transforms and the electrical model in isolation — no controller, no modulator, nothing that could mask a modelling error. It runs at a 10 µs step because nothing in it switches.

Only once that was trustworthy did I close the loops. The second model adds the inverter, the modulator and five PID loops, and drops to a 2 µs step so the switching instants land on the grid properly. Separating the two meant that when the closed-loop model misbehaved I already knew the plant underneath it was right.

sections.heading: Key features
sections.body:
- Dual-plane decomposition: fundamental (d1-q1) and third-harmonic (d3-q3) planes controlled independently
- Five regulators: outer speed loop, four inner current loops
- Loss-aware MTPA using Lagrange multipliers, solved by Newton-Raphson
- Flux weakening limited by the available DC-link voltage
- Five-phase SVPWM modulator driving a 10-switch two-level inverter
- Direct torque control with 20-sector hysteresis switching, as a comparison
- Load-torque step disturbance for testing transient response

sections.heading: Technologies
sections.body: MATLAB and Simulink, Simscape Electrical (Specialized Power Systems), Stateflow for the transform and modulator logic, Simulink Control Design for autotuning, and Code Composer Studio for the DSP target.

sections.heading: Software components
sections.body: A five-phase coordinate transform block pair (forward and inverse) handling both planes. A torque computation implementing the dual-plane expression. Five discrete PID regulators. An MTPA solver. An SVPWM modulator plus a comparison modulation path. Stateflow charts carrying the abc-to-dq and dq-to-abc mappings.

sections.heading: Technical detail
sections.body:
The transform uses the standard 2/5 scaling with 72° phase separation, so the fundamental plane maps on cos/sin of θe and the third-harmonic plane on cos/sin of 3θe. Torque comes out as

Te = (5P/4)·[ λm·iq1 + (Ld1−Lq1)·id1·iq1 + 3λm3·iq3 + (Ld3−Lq3)·id3·iq3 ]

The first two terms are the familiar magnet and reluctance torque; the second pair is the third-harmonic plane's contribution, which is why injecting third-harmonic current raises torque rather than just heating the machine.

Because Lq1 > Ld1, the reluctance term is only positive for negative id1, which is what sets the MTPA trajectory. Solving MTPA with a loss term rather than pure copper-loss minimisation has no closed form, hence the Newton-Raphson solver.

The closed-loop model runs fixed-step discrete at 2 µs. The switching period has to be an exact multiple of the step or the modulator jitters, which shows up as current ripple that looks like a tuning problem and isn't.

sections.heading: My contribution
sections.body:
I did the mathematical modelling and the simulation design. Professor Saifullah Payami and PhD scholar Amitesh Kumar provided a reference paper and a working three-phase reference model as the starting point.

Extending that to five phases was mine. A three-phase machine has one current plane; a five-phase machine has two, so the transform is not a matter of adding two more columns. I derived the five-phase Clarke and Park transforms myself — the fundamental plane on 72° spacing and the third-harmonic plane on 3θe, both with the 2/5 scaling — along with the dual-plane torque expression and the structure of the five regulators that sit on top of it.

sections.heading: Results
sections.body:
The closed-loop drive was run against a 1500 rpm (157 rad/s) speed reference with a 10 N·m load torque applied as a step at t = 5 s.

Speed reaches the 157 rad/s reference in about 0.2 s, with roughly 3.8% overshoot (peak ≈163 rad/s) and no steady-state error.
The load step produces no visible speed deviation at plot scale — the speed loop rejects it faster than the trace resolves.
Electromagnetic torque settles exactly on the 10 N·m load, after ≈32 N·m during acceleration.
q-axis current tracks torque demand: 15 A accelerating, ≈0 A unloaded, 4.7 A holding 10 N·m. Both figures give the same 2.13 N·m/A, which confirms the torque expression and the transform agree with each other.
d-axis current is held at zero throughout, and the third-harmonic plane currents stay within about ±0.9 A, so the second plane carries ripple only and no net current.

title: DC-DC boost converter
summary: Simulink model analysing steady-state and transient response across duty cycles and loads.
details: Open-loop boost converter modelled in Simscape Electrical: 20 V input, 10 kHz switching at 50% duty, 3.5 mH inductor and 572 µF output capacitor into a 200 Ω load
Measured 39.2 V output against the ideal Vin/(1−D) = 40 V, tracing the shortfall to the 0.8 V diode drop and the MOSFET's 0.1 Ω on-resistance
Verified continuous conduction mode: critical inductance is 1.25 mH, so the 3.5 mH choke holds inductor ripple to 0.29 A peak-to-peak on a 0.39 A average
Instrumented inductor, switch, diode and capacitor currents alongside inductor, switch and load voltages, with a Mean block averaging output voltage over one switching period

Diagnosed a startup failure mode: a lightly damped L-C pair (Q ≈ 40) driven by a hard duty step produced a 15 A inductor peak and 74 V output overshoot, both well beyond the ratings a 40 V, 0.4 A design would use
Fixed it by pre-charging the output capacitor to Vin and ramping duty from 0 to 0.5 over 100 ms through a PWM Generator, cutting the peak to 0.9 A and 40.1 V — a 17× reduction in inrush current

title: Weather dashboard
summary: Responsive app with live weather for any city and API error handling, deployed on Render.
details: Server-rendered Node/Express app with a POST route that queries the OpenWeatherMap current-weather API for any city
Renders seven live readings per lookup: temperature, humidity, visibility, wind speed, cloudiness, sunrise and sunset
Bootstrap offcanvas navigation and a mobile-first layout that collapses to a single column on phones
Unknown or misspelled city names return to the search form instead of throwing, so a bad lookup never crashes the server
Deployed on Render with the API key held in an environment variable rather than committed to the repository
